statement.p:
Let's look at two examples to develop some intuition for the concept of span.
First, we will consider the set of vectors
\vvec = \twovec{1}{2}, ~~~\wvec = \twovec{-2}{-4} .
An interactive diagram for constructing linear combinations of the vectors \vvec and \wvec.
An interactive for exploring linear combinations of two vectors.
There is a diagram with two vectors \vvec=twovec12 and \wvec=\twovec{-2}{-4} shown. These vectors lie on a line, which is also shown.
At the top of the diagram are two sliders, which allow the reader to vary two scalars c and d. The linear combination c\vvec+d\wvec is also shown. When either of the two sliders is changed, the new linear combination is shown.
The diagram below can be used to construct linear combinations whose weights c and d may be varied using the sliders at the top. The vectors \vvec and \wvec are outlined while the linear combination
c\vvec + d\wvec
is shaded in red.
There is an interactive diagram, available at , that accompanies this activity. The diagram at the top of that page accompanies part a of this activity.
What vector is the linear combination of \vvec and \wvec with weights:
c = 2 and d=0?
c = 1 and d=1?
c = 0 and d=-1?
Can the vector \twovec{2}{4} be expressed as a linear combination of \vvec and \wvec? Is the vector \twovec{2}{4} in the span of \vvec and \wvec?
Can the vector \twovec{3}{0} be expressed as a linear combination of \vvec and \wvec? Is the vector \twovec{3}{0} in the span of \vvec and \wvec?
Describe the set of vectors in the span of \vvec and \wvec.
For what vectors \bvec does the equation
\left[\begin{array}{rr} 1 \amp -2 \\ 2 \amp -4 \end{array}\right] \xvec = \bvec
have a solution?
We will now look at an example where
\vvec = \twovec{2}{1}, ~~~\wvec = \twovec{1}{2} .
An interactive diagram for constructing linear combinations of the vectors \vvec and \wvec.
An interactive for exploring linear combinations of two vectors.
There is a diagram with two vectors \vvec=twovec21 and \wvec=\twovec12 shown. There is also a grid consisting of two sets of parallel lines. One set of parallel lines is parallel to \vvec and passes through integer multiples of \wvec. The other set of parallel lines is parallel to \wvec and passes through integer multiples of \vvec.
At the top of the diagram are two sliders, which allow the reader to vary two scalars c and d. The linear combination c\vvec+d\wvec is also shown. When either of the two sliders is changed, the new linear combination is shown.
In a similar way, the diagram below can be used to construct linear combinations
c\vvec + d\wvec.

c = 2 and d=0?
c = 1 and d=1?
c = 0 and d=-1?
Can the vector \twovec{-2}{2} be expressed as a linear combination of \vvec and \wvec? Is the vector \twovec{-2}{2} in the span of \vvec and \wvec?
Can the vector \twovec{3}{0} be expressed as a linear combination of \vvec and \wvec? Is the vector \twovec{3}{0} in the span of \vvec and \wvec?
Describe the set of vectors in the span of \vvec and \wvec.
For what vectors \bvec does the equation
\left[\begin{array}{rr} 2 \amp 1 \\ 1 \amp 2 \end{array}\right] \xvec = \bvec
have a solution?

li.p:
For the first set of vectors, we find:
We can form the linear combinations:
When c = 2 and d=0, the linear combination is \twovec{2}{4}.
When c = 1 and d=1, the linear combination is \twovec{-1}{-2}.
When c = 0 and d=-1, the linear combination is \twovec{2}{4}.
Yes, we saw that there are at least two ways. For instance, when the weights are c=2 and d=0. This means that \twovec24 is in the span of \vvec and \wvec.
No. No matter how we change the weights, the linear combination lies on the line through \vvec and \wvec. This means that \twovec{3}{0} is not in the span of \vvec and \wvec.
The span of \vvec and \wvec is the set of all vectors on the line through \vvec.
If the equation has a solution, \bvec must lie on the line defined by \vvec.

For the second set of vectors, we have:
We can form the linear combinations:
When c = 2 and d=0, the linear combination is \twovec42.
When c = 1 and d=1, the linear combination is \twovec{3}{3}.
When c = 0 and d=-1, the linear combination is \twovec{-1}{-2}.
Yes. Using the diagram, we see that \twovec{-2}{2}=-2\vvec + 2\wvec. This means that \twovec{-2}{2} is in the span of \vvec and \wvec.
Yes. Using the diagram, we see that \twovec{3}{0}=2\vvec-1\wvec. This means that \twovec{3}{0} is in the span of \vvec and \wvec.
Every two-dimensional vector is in the span of \vvec and \wvec.
The equation has a solution for every \bvec.
